title: Tailored to Personas: Designing AI Assistant Responses
summary: How we built an intelligent documentation layer by grounding AI in a single source of truth and shaping the delivery to user intent
body_markdown:
Imagine two people logging into Guidewire documentation looking for the exact same solution:


A **Guidewire developer** needs to configure a Gosu rule, tweak an API integration, or check a data model constraint. Their priority is speed— *"Get me straight to the code snippet so I can build."* They skip long narratives in search of precise specs.


Across the aisle, a **P&C business analyst or product manager** is mapping out a new claim intake workflow or policy rating rule. Their priority is context— *"Show me how this functional block fits together so I can connect the dots."* They need structural framing before technical details make sense.


A single documentation page in enterprise platforms tries to be everything to everyone, but when these two roles land on the same page, their cognitive goals are different. To build an intelligent documentation layer that works, an AI assistant must ground its answers in a single source of truth while shaping the delivery to the persona's intent.


## The Speed and Detail Paradox


To build a truly helpful AI assistant, we have to look at how different roles process information. Recent user research into "time to information discovery" revealed a stark contrast in how technical and business readers consume docs:


- **The retrieval speed gap** : Technical experts locate key facts nearly 17 seconds faster on average than non-technical users because they rely on prior knowledge to skip straight to the specs.
- **The satisfaction mismatch** : When reading the exact same documentation, business users gave high marks (4.59 out of 5.00) to detailed textual explanations. Developers rated that same detail much lower (4.17), viewing long prose as unnecessary clutter.
- **The learner’s hurdle** : When documentation skips foundational context, business pathfinders hit a wall. Without a bridge connecting technical details to business value, tasks stall.


To bridge this gap, an AI assistant must classify both **who is asking** and their specific **user intent** , dynamically evaluating the response to deliver the exact depth, style, and format required.


## Designing the Experience: Two Core Interaction Frameworks


To make an AI assistant persona-aware, the underlying platform needs clear, role-based rules for how content is delivered:


### Content for Technical Experts


When generating answers for a developer or architect, the AI acts as a fast data-retrieval partner:


- **Lead with data** : Start with a clean summary box or table.
- **Code over prose** : Communicate using code blocks, parameter lists, and concise bullet points. Strip out conversational intro phrases like *"In this section, we will explore..."*
- **Direct links** : Provide inline links straight to deep-level API schemas rather than summarizing complex system concepts in long text.


### Content for Business Pathfinders


When answering a product manager or functional expert, the AI acts as a guide and conceptual tutor:


- **Focus on purpose** : Open with real-world use cases and business value.
- **Build a clear sequence** : Guide the reader from the high-level picture down to specific functional steps.
- **Translate jargon** : Define technical terms, endpoints, and variables in a business context.
- **Use visual supports** : Surface workflow diagrams, lifecycles, and quick summaries for visual learners.


## UX Guardrails: Balancing Automation with User Agency


Tailoring AI responses creates a better experience, but personalization should never feel restrictive. User testing shows that a successful AI assistant requires three guardrails:


- **Persistent control** : Users want to set their default role or preferences once and have them stick across sessions. Explicit profile controls give users confidence that the system respects their preferences.
- **Flexible filtering** : Collaboration is key. A developer might need a high-level functional overview to hand off to an analyst, while an analyst might need to check a code parameter. The UI needs an easy toggle to temporarily switch roles without hassle.
- **Transparent filtering** : Personalization shouldn't be invisible. If a user gets a summarized answer because their profile is set to a business role, but they are trying to run a technical query, they might think the AI lacks depth. Always show which filters are active.


## Better Wayfinding for Every User


Dynamic, persona-aware delivery ensures that comprehensive documentation works seamlessly for everyone across the P&C lifecycle. By evaluating **user intent** alongside role-based preferences, AI acts as an intelligent layer between the single source of truth and the user.


Whether a developer needs a precise Gosu snippet or an analyst needs to map out a claim workflow, getting the right depth of detail helps teams move faster, reduce cognitive load, and get the most out of their enterprise platform.
